paragraphs.text: A 2008 cake of [raw pu’er](sheng:identity) from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, on the east side of the Lancang River. The area is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and its town has long been where leaf from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed. The record names the region rather than a single village, and [on a label the name](greater-yiwu:on-a-label) can mean the town, the mountain or a wider area.

Raw pu’er is fried to kill the green and then [dried in the sun](sheng:making) rather than by hot air, so some of the leaf’s own activity survives and the tea keeps changing for years. How fast depends on how tightly it was [pressed](sheng:pressing) and how it was [stored](sheng:storage), since heat and humidity drive the slow oxidation and microbial work inside the cake.
At eighteen years this cake sits where the trade divides: some count raw pu’er as [aged](sheng:ageing) from ten years, while many wait for twenty or more.

brewing.text: Pry the leaf off a cake or brick in chunks with a pick or knife, from the surface and toward the centre, rather than crumbling it. A mix of larger pieces and smaller ones brews evenly. Young raw pu’er takes water a little off the boil, about 85 to 95°C, because hotter water draws out more of its bitterness; an aged one takes 95°C to boiling. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and a quick rinse of a few seconds, then a first steep of ten to fifteen seconds, adding a few seconds each round. A good raw tea gives eight to ten cups or more.

notice.text: A smoother, thicker, sweeter cup with woody, herbal and camphor notes and something of dried dates or dark fruit.
